glint: A glimpse, glance, or gleam. [Scot.] "He saw a glint of light." Ramsay. | To glance; to peep forth, as a flower from the bud; to glitter. Burns.
gladius: The internal shell, or pen, of cephalopods like the squids.
glover: One whose trade it is to make or sell gloves. Glover's suture or stitch, a kind of stitch used in sewing up wounds, in which the thread is drawn alternately through each side from within outward.
glutaconic: Pertaining to, or derived from, an acid intermediate between glutaric and aconitic acids.
glamour: 1. A charm affecting the eye, making objects appear different from what they really are. 2. Witchcraft; magic; a spell. Tennyson. 3. A kind of haze in the air, causing things to appear different from what they really are. The air filled with a strange, pale glamour that seemed to lie over the broad valley. W. Black. 4.
glengarry: A kind of Highland Scotch cap for men, with straight sides and a hollow top sloping to the back, where it is parted and held together by ribbons or strings. The long silk streamers of his Glengarry bonnet. L. Hutton.
globefish: A plectognath fish of the genera Diodon, Tetrodon, and allied genera. The globefishes can suck in water or air and distend the body to a more or less globular form. Called also porcupine fish, and sea hedgehog. See Diodon.
glochidiate: Having barbs; as, glochidiate bristles. Gray.
glimmering: 1. Faint, unsteady light; a glimmer. South. 2. A faint view or idea; a glimpse; an inkling.
glossal: Of or pertaining to the tongue; lingual.
glonoine: 1. Same as Nitroglycerin; -- called also oil of glonoin. (old) 2. (Med.) A dilute solution of nitroglycerin used as a neurotic.
glowlamp: 1. (Chem.) An aphlogistic lamp. See Aphlogistic. 2. (Elect.) An incandescent lamp. See Incandescent, a.
globose: Having a rounded form resembling that of a globe; globular, or nearly so; spherical. Milton.
glucinic: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, glucinum; as, glucinic oxide.
glandular: Containing or supporting glands; consisting of glands; pertaining to glands.
glycoluric: Pertaining to, derived from, glycol and urea; as, glycoluric acid, which is called also hydantoic acid.
gland: 1. (Anat.) (a) An organ for secreting something to be used in, or eliminated from, the body; as, the sebaceous glands of the skin; the salivary glands of the mouth. (b) An organ or part which resembles a secreting, or true, gland, as the ductless, lymphatic, pineal, and pituitary glands, the functions of which are very imperfectly known.
glumella: One of the pelets or inner chaffy scales of the flowers or spikelets of grasses.
gleeman: A name anciently given to an itinerant minstrel or musician.
glyoxaline: A white, crystalline, organic base, C3H4N2, produced by the action of ammonia on glyoxal, and forming the origin of a large class of derivatives hence, any one of the series of which glyoxaline is a type; -- called also oxaline.
gloss: 1. Bbrightness or luster of a body proceeding from a smooth surface; polish; as, the gloss of silk; cloth is calendered to give it a gloss. It is no part . . . to set on the face of this cause any… | To give a superficial luster or gloss to; to make smooth and shining; as, to gloss cloth. The glossed and gleamy wave. J. R. Drake.
glassmaker: One who makes, or manufactures, glass. -- Glass" mak`ing, or Glass"mak`ing, n.
glomuliferous: Having small clusters of minutely branched coral-like excrescences. M. C. Cooke.
glaucoma: Dimness or abolition of sight, with a diminution of transparency, a bluish or greenish tinge of the refracting media of the eye, and a hard inelastic condition of the eyeball, with marked increase of tension within the eyeball.
gloomy: 1. Imperfectly illuminated; dismal through obscurity or darkness; dusky; dim; clouded; as, the cavern was gloomy. "Though hid in gloomiest shade." Milton. 2. Affected with, or expressing, gloom; melancholy; dejected; as, a gloomy temper or countenance. Syn. -- Dark; dim; dusky; dismal; cloudy; moody; sullen; morose; melancholy; sad; downcast; depressed; dejected; disheartened.
glassware: Ware, or articles collectively, made of glass.
globule: 1. A little globe; a small particle of matter, of a spherical form. Globules of snow. Sir I. Newton. These minute globules [a mole's eyes] are sunk . . . deeply in the skull. Paley. 2. (Biol.) A minute spherical or rounded structure; as blood, lymph, and pus corpuscles, minute fungi, spores, etc. 3. A little pill or pellet used by homeopathists.
glassite: A member of a Scottish sect, founded in the 18th century by John Glass, a minister of the Established Church of Scotland, who taught that justifying faith is "no more than a simple assent to the divine testimone passively recived by the understanding." The English and American adherents of this faith are called Sandemanians, after Robert Sandeman, the son-in-law and disciple…
gleg: Quick of perception; alert; sharp. [Scot.] Jamieson.
glumpy: Glum; sullen; sulky. [Colloq.] "He was glumpy enough." T. Hook.
glauberite: A mineral, consisting of the sulphates of soda and lime. GLAUBER'S SALT; GLAUBER'S SALTS Glau"ber's salt` or; Glau"ber's salts` (. Etym: [G. glaubersalz, from Glauber, a German chemist who discovered it. See Glauberite.] Sulphate of soda, a well-known cathartic.
glucinum: A rare metallic element, of a silver white color, and low specific gravity (2.1), resembling magnesium. It never occurs naturally in the free state, but is always combined, usually with silica or alumina, or both; as in the minerals phenacite, chrysoberyl, beryl or emerald, euclase, and danalite.
glyoxal: A white, amorphous, deliquescent powder, (CO.H)2, obtained by the partial oxidation of glycol. It is a double aldehyde, between glycol and oxalic acid.
glockenspiel: An instrument, originally a series of bells on an iron rod, now a set of flat metal bars, diatonically tuned, giving a bell-like tone when played with a mallet; a carillon.
glyphography: A process similar to etching, in which, by means of voltaic electricity, a raised copy of a drawing is made, so that it can be used to print from.
glomerate: Gathered together in a roundish mass or dense cluster; conglomerate. | To gather or wind into a ball; to collect into a spherical form or mass, as threads.
gladiatorship: Conduct, state, or art, of a gladiator.
glyphic: Of or pertaining to sculpture or carving of any sort, esp. to glyphs.
glove: 1. A cover for the hand, or for the hand and wrist, with a separate sheath for each finder. The latter characteristic distinguishes the glove from the mitten. 2. A boxing glove. Boxing glove. | To cover with, or as with, a glove.
glabrous: Smooth; having a surface without hairs or any unevenness.
glombe: To gloom; to look gloomy, morose, or sullen. (old) Surrey.
glyptic: 1. Of or pertaining to gem engraving. 2. (Min.) Figured; marked as with figures.
glastonburythorn: A variety of the common hawthorn. Loudon.
glycyrrhizin: A glucoside found in licorice root (Glycyrrhiza), in monesia bark (Chrysophyllum), in the root of the walnut, etc., and extracted as a yellow, amorphous powder, of a bittersweet taste.
glucoside: One of a large series of amorphous or crystalline substances, occurring very widely distributed in plants, rarely in animals, and regarded as influental agents in the formation and disposition of the sugars.
globularity: The state of being globular; globosity; sphericity.
glowworm: A coleopterous insect of the genus Lampyris; esp., the wingless females and larvæ of the two European species (L. noctiluca, and L. splendidula), which emit light from some of the abdominal segments. Like a glowworm in the night, The which hath fire in darkness, none in light. Shak. Note: The male is winged, and is supposed to be attracted by the light of the female.
gleba: The chambered sporogenous tissue forming the central mass of the sporophore in puff balls, stinkhorns, etc.
gleamy: Darting beams of light; casting light in rays; flashing; coruscating. In brazed arms, that cast a gleamy ray, Swift through the town the warrior bends his way. Pope.
globated: Having the form of a globe; spherical.
glutaric: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid so called; as, glutaric ethers. Glutaric acid, an organic acid obtained as a white crystalline substance, isomeric with pyrotartaric acid; -- called also normal pyrotartaric acid.
glaciate: 1. To convert into, or cover with, ice. 2. (Geol.) To produce glacial effects upon, as in the scoring of rocks, transportation of loose material, etc. Glaciated rocks, rocks whose surfaces have been smoothed, furrowed, or striated, by the action of ice.
glaum: To grope with the hands, as in the dark. [Scot.] To glaum at, to grasp or snatch at; to aspire to. Wha glaum'd at kingdoms three. Burns.
glandage: A feeding on nuts or mast. (old) Crabb.
glancingly: In a glancing manner; transiently; incidentally; indirectly. Hakewill.
glossarially: In the manner of a glossary.
glyn: A glen. See Glen. Note: [Obs. singly, but occurring often in locative names in Ireland, as Glen does in Scotland.] He could not beat out the Irish, yet he did shut them up within those narrow corners and glyns under the mountain's foot. Spenser.
glyceride: A compound ether (formed from glycerin). Some glycerides exist ready formed as natural fats, others are produced artificially.
glostoven: An oven in which glazed pottery is fired; -- also called glaze kiln, or glaze.
glen: A secluded and narrow valley; a dale; a depression between hills. And wooes the widow's daughter of the glen. Spenser.
glow: 1. To shine with an intense or white heat; to give forth vivid light and heat; to be incandenscent. Glows in the stars, and blossoms in the trees. Pope. 2. To exhibit a strong, bright color; | To make hot; to flush. (poetic) Fans, whose wind did seem To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool. Shak.
glanders: A highly contagious and very destructive disease of horses, asses, mules, etc., characterized by a constant discharge of sticky matter from the nose, and an enlargement and induration of the glands beneath and within the lower jaw. It may transmitted to dogs, goats, sheep, and to human beings.
glandiform: Having the form of a gland or nut; resembling a gland.
gleek: 1. A jest or scoff; a trick or deception. (old) Where's the Bastard's braves, and Charles his gleeks Shak. 2. Etym: [Cf. Glicke] An enticing look or glance. (old) A pretty gleek coming from Pallas'… | To make sport; to gibe; to sneer; to spend time idly. (old) Shak.
glume: The bracteal covering of the flowers or seeds of grain and grasses; esp., an outer husk or bract of a spikelt. Gray.
glasscrab: The larval state (Phyllosoma) of the genus Palinurus and allied genera. It is remarkable for its strange outlines, thinness, and transparency. See Phyllosoma.
glyoxime: A white, crystalline, nitrogenous substance, produced by the action of hydroxylamine on glyoxal, and belonging to the class of oximes; also, any one of a group of substances resembling glyoxime proper, and of which it is a type. See Oxime.
glair: 1. The white of egg. It is used as a size or a glaze in bookbinding, for pastry, etc. 2. Any viscous, transparent substance, resembling the white of an egg. 3. A broadsword fixed on a pike; | To smear with the white of an egg.
glossary: A collection of glosses or explanations of words and passages of a work or author; a partial dictionary of a work, an author, a dialect, art, or science, explaining archaic, technical, or other uncommon words.
glorify: 1. To make glorious by bestowing glory upon; to confer honor and distinction upon; to elevate to power or happiness, or to celestial glory. Jesus was not yet glorified. John vii. 39. 2. To make glorious in thought or with the heart, by ascribing glory to; to asknowledge the excellence of; to render homage to; to magnify in worship; to adore.
glassgazing: Given to viewing one's self in a glass or mirror; finical. (poetic) Shak.
gladstone: A four-wheeled pleasure carriage with two inside seats, calash top, and seats for driver and footman.
glibly: In a glib manner; as, to speak glibly.
glaver: 1. To prate; to jabber; to babble. (old) Here many, clepid filosophirs, glavern diversely. Wyclif. 2. To flatter; to wheedle. (old) Some slavish, glavering, flattering parasite. South.
glyptodont: One of a family (glyptodontidæ) of extinct South American edentates, of which Glyptodon is the type. About twenty species are known.
gleam: 1. A shoot of light; a small stream of light; a beam; a ray; a glimpse. Transient unexpected gleams of joi. Addison. At last a gleam Of dawning light turned thitherward in haste His [Satan's]… | 1. To shoot, or dart, as rays of light; as, at the dawn, light gleams in the east. 2. To shine; to cast light; to glitter. Syn. -- To Gleam, Glimmer, Glitter. To gleam denotes a faint but distinct…
glebe: 1. A lump; a clod. 2. Turf; soil; ground; sod. Fertile of corn the glebe, of oil, and wine. Milton. 3. (Eccl. Law) The land belonging, or yielding revenue, to a parish church or ecclesiastical benefice.
glyoxalic: Pertaining to, or designating, an aldehyde acid, intermediate between glycol and oxalic acid. [Written also glyoxylic.]
glebous: Pertaining to the glebe; turfy; cloddy; fertile; fruitful. "Gleby land." Prior.
glycose: One of a class of carbohydrates having from three to nine atoms of carbon in the molecules and having the constitution either of an aldehyde alcohol or of a ketone alcohol. Most glycoses have hydrogen and oxygen present in the proportion to form water, while the number of carbon atoms is usually equal to the number of atoms of oxygen.
glasssnake: A long, footless lizard (Ophiosaurus ventralis), of the Southern United States; -- so called from its fragility, the tail easily breaking into small pieces. It grows to the length of three feet. The name is applied also to similar species found in the Old World.
gluttonous: Given to gluttony; eating to excess; indulging the appetite; voracious; as, a gluttonous age. -- Glut"ton*ous*ly, adv. -- Glut"ton*ous*ness, n.
gliff: 1. A transient glance; an unexpected view of something that startles one; a sudden fear. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell. 2. A moment: as, for a gliff. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
glider: One who, or that which, glides.
glasswork: Manufacture of glass; articles or ornamentation made of glass.
gladiate: Sword-shaped; resembling a sword in form, as the leaf of the iris, or of the gladiolus.
glaucodot: A metallic mineral having a grayish tin-white color, and containing cobalt and iron, with sulphur and arsenic.
gleaning: The act of gathering after reapers; that which is collected by gleaning. Glenings of natural knowledge. Cook.
glucina: A white or gray tasteless powder, the oxide of the element glucinum; -- formerly called glucine.
glycogeny: The production or formation of sugar from gycogen, as in the liver.
gladiator: 1. Originally, a swordplayer; hence, one who fought with weapons in public, either on the occasion of a funeral ceremony, or in the arena, for public amusement. 2. One who engages in any fierce combat or controversy.
glaucic: Of or pertaining to the Glaucium or horned poppy; -- formerly applied to an acid derived from it, now known to be fumaric acid.
glandulous: Containing glands; consisting of glands; pertaining to glands; resembling glands.
glaucine: An alkaloid obtained from the plant Glaucium, as a bitter, white, crystalline substance.
glires: An order of mammals; the Rodentia. -- Gli"rine, a.
glossohyal: Pertaining to both the hyoidean arch and the tongue; -- applied to the anterior segment of the hyoidean arch in many fishes. -- n. The glossohyal bone or cartilage; lingual bone; entoglossal bone.
gladsome: 1. Pleased; joyful; cheerful. 2. Causing joy, pleasure, or cheerfulness; having the appearance of gayety; pleasing. Of opening heaven they sung, and gladsome day. Prior. -- Glad"some*ly, adv. -- Glad"some*ness, n. Hours of perfect gladsomeness. Wordsworth.
globate: Having the form of a globe; spherical.
glasssponge: A siliceous sponge, of the genus Hyalonema, and allied genera; -- so called from their glassy fibers or spicules; -- called also vitreous sponge. See Glass-rope, and Euplectella.
glim: 1. Brightness; splendor. (old) 2. A light or candle. [Slang] Dickens. Douse the glim, put out the light. [Slang]
glee: 1. Music; minstrelsy; entertainment. (old) Chaucer. 2. Joy; merriment; mirth; gayety; paricularly, the mirth enjoyed at a feast. Spenser. 3. (Mus.) An unaccompanied part song for three or more solo voices. It is not necessarily gleesome.
glyconin: An emulsion of glycerin and the yolk of eggs, used as an ointment, as a vehicle for medicines, etc.
glyceric: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycerin. Glyceric acid (Chem.), an organic acid, obtained by the partial oxidation of glycerin, as a thick liquid. It is a hydroxyl derivative of propionic acid, and has both acid and alcoholic properties.
glandule: A small gland or secreting vessel.
glycocholate: A salt of glycocholic acid; as, sodium glycocholate.
glidingangle: The angle, esp. the least angle, at which a gliding machine or aëroplane will glide to earth by virtue of gravity without applied power.
glyptography: The art or process of engraving on precious stones.
glue: A hard brittle brownish gelatin, obtained by boiling to a jelly the skins, hoofs, etc., of animals. When gently heated with water, it becomes viscid and tenaceous, and is used as a cement for uniting… | To join with glue or a viscous substance; to cause to stick or hold fast, as if with glue; to fix or fasten. This cold, congealed blood That glues my lips, and will not let me speak. Shak.
glossarial: Of or pertaining to glosses or to a glossary; containing a glossary.
glabriate: To make smooth, plain, or bare. (old)
globulin: An albuminous body, insoluble in water, but soluble in dilute solutions of salt. It is present in the red blood corpuscles united with hæmatin to form hæmoglobin. It is also found in the crystalline lens of the eye, and in blood serum, and is sometimes called crystallin.
glare: 1. To shine with a bright, dazzling light. The cavern glares with new-admitted light. Dryden. 2. To look with fierce, piercing eyes; to stare earnestly, angrily, or fiercely. | To shoot out, or emit, as a dazzling light. Every eye Glared lightning, and shot forth pernicious fire. Milton.
glycocholic: Pertaining to, or composed of, glycocoll and cholic acid. Glycocholic acid (Physiol. Chem.), a conjugate acid, composed of glycocoll and cholic acid, present in bile in the form of a sodium salt. The acid commonly forms a resinous mass, but can be crystallized in long, white needles.
glenoid: Having the form of a smooth and shallow depression; sockas, the glenoid cavity, or fossa, of the scapula, in which the head of the humerus articulates.
glyptotheca: A building or room devoted to works of sculpture.
glottic: Of or pertaining to the glottis; glottal.
glycocoll: A crystalline, nitrogenous substance, with a sweet taste, formed from hippuric acid by boiling with hydrochloric acid, and present in bile united with cholic acid. It is also formed from gelatin by decomposition with acids. Chemically, it is amido-acetic acid. Called also glycin, and glycocin.
glorious: 1. Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory; noble; praiseworthy; excellent; splendid; illustrious; inspiring admiration; as, glorious deeds. These are thy glorious works, Parent of good ! Milton. 2. Eager for glory or distinction; haughty; boastful; ostentatious; vainglorious. (old) Most miserable Is the desire that's glorious. Shak. 3.
glycolyl: A divalent, compound radical, CO.CH2, regarded as the essential radical of glycolic acid, and a large series of related compounds.
glazy: Having a glazed appearance; -- said of the fractured surface of some kinds of pin iron.
glyptodon: An extinct South American quaternary mammal, allied to the armadillos. It was as large as an ox, was covered with tessellated scales, and had fluted teeth. Owen.
glary: Of a dazzling luster; glaring; bright; shining; smooth. Bright, crystal glass is glary. Boyle.
glenlivat: A kind of Scotch whisky, named from the district in which it was first made. W. E. Aytoun.
gleet: A transparent mucous discharge from the membrane of the urethra, commonly an effect of gonorrhea. Hoblyn. | 1. To flow in a thin, limpid humor; to ooze, as gleet. Wiseman. 2. To flow slowly, as water. Cheyne.
gladful: Full of gladness; joyful; glad. -- Glad"ful*ness, n. Spenser. It followed him with gladful glee. Spenser.
glyptographic: Relating to glyptography, or the art of engraving on precious stones.
glassfaced: Mirror-faced; reflecting the sentiments of another. "The glass-faced flatterer." Shak.
gloria: (a) A doxology (beginning Gloria Patri, Glory be to the Father), sung or said at the end of the Psalms in the service of the Roman Catholic and other churches. (b) A portion of the Mass (Gloria in Excelsis Deo, Glory be to God on high), and also of the communion service in some churches. In the Episcopal Church the version in English is used.
glide: 1. To move gently and smoothly; to pass along without noise, violence, or apparent effort; to pass rapidly and easily, or with a smooth, silent motion, as a river in its channel, a bird in the air, a… | 1. The act or manner of moving smoothly, swiftly, and without labor or obstruction. They prey at last ensnared, he dreadful darts, With rapid glide, along the leaning line. Thomson.
glyptics: The art of engraving on precious stones.
gloriosa: A genus of climbing plants with very showy lilylike blossoms, natives of India.
gladden: To make glad; to cheer; to please; to gratify; to rejoice; to exhilarate. A secret pleasure gladdened all that saw him. Addison. | To be or become glad; to rejoice. The vast Pacific gladdens with the freight. Wordsworth.
glaive: 1. A weapon formerly used, consisting of a large blade fixed on the end of a pole, whose edge was on the outside curve; also, a light lance with a long sharp-pointed head. Wilhelm. 2. A sword; -- used poetically and loosely. The glaive which he did wield. Spenser.
glidder: Giving no sure footing; smooth; slippery. [Prov. Eng.] Shingle, slates, and gliddery stones. R. D. Blackmore.
glossanthrax: A disease of horses and cattle accompanied by carbuncles in the mouth and on the tongue.
glumal: Characterized by a glume, or having the nature of a glume.
glabella: The space between the eyebrows, also including the corresponding part of the frontal bone; the mesophryon. -- Gla*bel"lar, a.
glimmer: To give feeble or scattered rays of light; to shine faintly; to show a faint, unsteady light; as, the glimmering dawn; a glimmering lamp. The west yet glimmers with some streaks of day. Shak. Syn. | 1. A faint, unsteady light; feeble, scattered rays of light; also, a gleam. Gloss of satin and glimmer of pearls. Tennyson. 2. Mica. See Mica. Woodsward. Glimmer gowk, an owl. [Prov. Eng.] Tennyson.
gliddery: Giving no sure footing; smooth; slippery. [Prov. Eng.] Shingle, slates, and gliddery stones. R. D. Blackmore.
glossology: 1. The definition and explanation of terms; a glossary. 2. The science of language; comparative philology; linguistics; glottology.
gladly: 1. Preferably; by choice. (old) Chaucer. 2. With pleasure; joyfully; cheerfully; eagerly. The common people heard him gladly. Mark xii. 37.
glama: A copious gummy secretion of the humor of the eyelids, in consequence of some disorder; blearedness; lippitude.
gloaming: 1. Twilight; dusk; the fall of the evening. [Scot. & North of Eng., and in poetry.] Hogg. 2. Sullenness; melancholy. (old) J. Still.
glory: 1. Praise, honor, admiration, or distinction, accorded by common consent to a person or thing; high reputation; honorable fame; renown. Glory to God in the highest. Luke ii. 14. | 1. To exult with joy; to rejoice. Glory ye in his holy name. Ps. cv. 2. To boast; to be proud. God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Gal. vi. 14 No one . . .
gloze: 1. To flatter; to wheedle; to fawn; to talk smoothly. Chaucer. A false, glozing parasite. South. So glozed the tempter, and his proem tuned. Milton. 2. To give a specious or false meaning; | To smooth over; to palliate. By glozing the evil that is in the world. I. Taylor.
gladiatorian: Of or pertaining to gladiators, or to contests or combatants in general.
glasshouse: A house where glass is made; a commercial house that deals in glassware.
glum: Moody; silent; sullen. I frighten people by my glun face. Thackeray. | To look sullen; to be of a sour countenance; to be glum. (old) Hawes.
glean: 1. To gather after a reaper; to collect in scattered or fragmentary parcels, as the grain left by a reaper, or grapes left after the gathering. To glean the broken ears after the man That the main… | 1. To gather stalks or ears of grain left by reapers. And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers. Ruth ii. 3. 2. To pick up or gather anything by degrees.
gleby: Pertaining to the glebe; turfy; cloddy; fertile; fruitful. "Gleby land." Prior.
glister: To be bright; to sparkle; to be brilliant; to shine; to glisten; to glitter. All that glisters is not gold. Shak.
glycosine: An organic base, C6H6N4, produced artificially as a white, crystalline powder, by the action of ammonia on glyoxal.
glibbery: 1. Slippery; changeable. (old) My love is glibbery; there is no hold on't. Marston. 2. Moving easily; nimble; voluble. (old) Thy lubrical and glibbery muse. B. Jonson.
globiferous: Having a round or globular tip.
glomeration: 1. The act of forming or gathering into a ball or round mass; the state of being gathered into a ball; conglomeration. 2. That which is formed into a ball; a ball. Bacon.
glandulation: The situation and structure of the secretory vessels in plants. Martyn. Glandulation respects the secretory vessels, which are either glandules, follicles, or utricles. J. Lee.
glutinative: Having the quality of cementing; tenacious; viscous; glutinous.
glaciation: 1. Act of freezing. 2. That which is formed by freezing; ice. 3. The process of glaciating, or the state of being glaciated; the production of glacial phenomena.
globuliferous: Bearing globules; in geology, used of rocks, and denoting a variety of concretionary structure, where the concretions are isolated globules and evenly distributed through the texture of the rock.
glycosometer: An apparatus for determining the amount of sugar in diabetic urine.
glazier: One whose business is to set glass. Glazier's diamond. See under Diamond.
glandiferous: Bearing acorns or other nuts; as, glandiferous trees.
globeflower: (a) A plant of the genus Trollius (T. Europæus), found in the mountainous parts of Europe, and producing handsome globe-shaped flowers. (b) The American plant Trollius laxus. Japan globeflower. See Corchorus.
glade: 1. An open passage through a wood; a grassy open or cleared space in a forest. There interspersed in lawns and opening glades. Pope. 2. An everglade. [Local, U. S.] 3. An opening in the ice of rivers or lakes, or a place left unfrozen; also, smooth ice. [Local, U. S.] Bottom glade. See under Bottom.
gladiole: A lilylike plant, of the genus Gladiolus; -- called also corn flag.
glaucescent: Having a somewhat glaucous appearance or nature; becoming glaucous.
glycolic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycol; as, glycolic ether; glycolic acid. Glycolic acid (Chem.), an organic acid, found naturally in unripe grapes and in the leaves of the wild grape (Ampelopsis quinquefolia), and produced artificially in many ways, as by the oxidation of glycol, -- whence its name.
glossa: The tongue, or lingua, of an insect. See Hymenoptera.
globy: Resembling, or pertaining to, a globe; round; orbicular. "The globy sea." Milton.
glottal: Of or pertaining to, or produced by, the glottis; glottic. Glottal catch, an effect produced upon the breath or voice by a sudden opening or closing of the glotts. Sweet.
glomerule: 1. (Bot.) A head or dense cluster of flowers, formed by condensation of a cyme, as in the flowering dogwood. 2. (Anat.) A glomerulus.
gleeclub: A club or company organized for singing glees, and (by extension) part songs, ballads, etc.
glaucophane: A mineral of a dark bluish color, related to amphibole. It is characteristic of certain crystalline rocks.
glumly: In a glum manner; sullenly; moodily.
glenlivet: A kind of Scotch whisky, named from the district in which it was first made. W. E. Aytoun.
glasssnail: A small, transparent, land snail, of the genus Vitrina.
glycogenic: Pertaining to, or caused by, glycogen; as, the glycogenic function of the liver.
glass: 1. A hard, brittle, translucent, and commonly transparent substance, white or colored, having a conchoidal fracture, and made by fusing together sand or silica with lime, potash, soda, or lead oxide. | 1. To reflect, as in a mirror; to mirror; -- used reflexively. Happy to glass themselves in such a mirror. Motley. Where the Almighty's form glasses itself in tempests. Byron. 2. To case in glass.
glycolide: A white amorphous powder, C4H4O, obtained by heating and dehydrating glycolic acid. [Written also glycollide.]
glome: To gloom; to look gloomy, morose, or sullen. (old) Surrey. | One of the two prominences at the posterior extremity of the frog of the horse's foot.
glutinosity: The quality of being glutinous; viscousness.
globigerina: A genus of small Foraminifera, which live abundantly at or near the surface of the sea. Their dead shells, falling to the bottom, make up a large part of the soft mud, generally found in depths below 3,000 feet, and called globigerina ooze. See Illust. of Foraminifera.
gluttonize: To eat to excess; to eat voraciously; to gormandize. Hallywell.
glaring: Clear; notorious; open and bold; barefaced; as, a glaring crime. -- Glar"ing*ly, adv.
glans: 1. (Anat.) The vascular body which forms the apex of the penis, and the extremity of the clitoris. 2. (Bot.) The acorn or mast of the oak and similar fruits. Gray. 3. (Med.) (a) Goiter. (b) A pessary. (old)
gladiolus: 1. (Bot.) A genus of plants having bulbous roots and gladiate leaves, and including many species, some of which are cultivated and valued for the beauty of their flowers; the corn flag; the sword lily. 2. (Anat.) The middle portion of the sternum in some animals; the mesosternum.
gloriation: Boast; a triumphing. (old) Bp. Richardson. Internal gloriation or triumph of the mind. Hobbes.
gleucometer: An instrument for measuring the specific gravity and ascertaining the quantity of sugar contained in must.
glut: 1. To swallow, or to swallow greedlly; to gorge. Though every drop of water swear against it, And gape at widest to glut him. Shak. 2. To fill to satiety; to satisfy fully the desire or craving of; | To eat gluttonously or to satiety. Like three horses that have broken fence, And glutted all night long breast-deep in corn. Tennyson.
glacious: Pertaining to, consisting of or resembling, ice; icy. Sir T. Browne.
glossographer: A writer of a glossary; a commentator; a scholiast. Hayward.
glossopharyngeal: Pertaining to both the tongue and the pharynx; -- applied especially to the ninth pair of cranial nerves, which are distributed to the pharynx and tongue. -- n. One of the glossopharyngeal nerves.
glowingly: In a glowing manner; with ardent heat or passion.
gloam: 1. To begin to grow dark; to grow dusky. 2. To be sullen or morose. (old) | The twilight; gloaming. Keats.
globulimeter: An instrument for measuring the number of red blood corpuscles in the blood. Note: The method depends on the differences of tint obtained by mixing a sample of the blood with sodium carbonate solution.
glengarrybonnet: A kind of Highland Scotch cap for men, with straight sides and a hollow top sloping to the back, where it is parted and held together by ribbons or strings. The long silk streamers of his Glengarry bonnet. L. Hutton.
gluttony: Excess in eating; extravagant indulgence of the appetite for food; voracity. Their sumptuous gluttonies, and gorgeous feasts. Milton.
glossator: A writer of glosses or comments; a commentator. "The . . . glossators of Aristotle." Milman.
glairy: Like glair, or partaking of its qualities; covered with glair; viscous and transparent; slimy. Wiseman.
glyphograph: A plate made by glyphography, or an impression taken from such a plate.
glabrate: Becoming smooth or glabrous from age. Gray.
glycerin: An oily, viscous liquid, C3H5(OH)3, colorless and odorless, and with a hot, sweetish taste, existing in the natural fats and oils as the base, combined with various acids, as oleic, margaric, stearic, and palmitic. It is a triatomic alcohol, and hence is also called glycerol. See Note under Gelatin.
glucose: 1. A variety of sugar occurring in nature very abundantly, as in ripe grapes, and in honey, and produced in great quantities from starch, etc., by the action of heat and acids. It is only about half as sweet as cane sugar. Called also dextrose, grape sugar, diabetic sugar, and starch sugar. See Dextrose. 2.
glycogenesis: The production or formation of sugar from gycogen, as in the liver.
glutamic: Of or pertaining to gluten. Glutamic acid, a nitrogenous organic acid obtained from certain albuminoids, as gluten; -- called also amido-glutaric acid.C5H9NO4.
glutinous: 1. Of the nature of glue; resembling glue; viscous; viscid; adhesive; gluey. 2. (Bot.) Havig a moist and adhesive or sticky surface, as a leaf or gland.
gloat: To look steadfastly; to gaz In vengeance gloating on another's pain. Byron.
glomerous: Gathered or formed into a ball or round mass. (old) Blount.
glunch: Frowning; sulky; sullen. Sir W. Scott. -- n. A sullen, angry look; a look of disdain or dislike. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
glumelle: One of the pelets or inner chaffy scales of the flowers or spikelets of grasses.
glitter: 1. To sparkle with light; to shine with a brilliant and broken light or showy luster; to gleam; as, a glittering sword. The field yet glitters with the pomp of war. Dryden. 2. | A bright, sparkling light; brilliant and showy luster; brilliancy; as, the glitter of arms; the glitter of royal equipage. Milton.
glancing: 1. Shooting, as light. When through the gancing lightnings fly. Rowe. 2. Flying off (after striking) in an oblique direction; as, a glancing shot.
glycogen: A white, amorphous, tasteless substance resembling starch, soluble in water to an opalescent fluid. It is found abundantly in the liver of most animals, and in small quantity in other organs and tissues, particularly in the embryo. It is quickly changed into sugar when boiled with dilute sulphuric or hydrochloric acid, and also by the action of amylolytic ferments.
gluconic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glucose. Gluconic acid (Chem.), an organic acid, obtained as a colorless, sirupy liquid, by the oxidation of glucose; -- called also maltonic acid, and dextronic acid.
glochidium: The larva or young of the mussel, formerly thought to be a parasite upon the parent's gills.
glorification: 1. The act of glorifyng or of giving glory to. Jer. Taylor. 2. The state of being glorifed; as, the glorification of Christ after his resurrection.
globular: Globe-shaped; having the form of a ball or sphere; spherical, or nearly so; as, globular atoms. Milton. Globular chart, a chart of the earth's surface constructed on the principles of the globular projection.
glad: 1. Pleased; joyous; happy; cheerful; gratified; -- opposed to sorry, sorrowful, or unhappy; -- said of persons, and often followed by of, at, that, or by the infinitive, and sometimes by with,… | To make glad; to cheer; to gladden; to exhilarate. Chaucer. That which gladded all the warrior train. Dryden. Each drinks the juice that glads the heart of man. Pope.
glacialist: One who attributes the phenomena of the drift, in geology, to glaciers.
glace: Coated with icing; iced; glazed; -- said of fruits, sweetmeats, cake, etc.
gladiatorism: The art or practice of a gladiator.
glucic: Pertaining to, or obtained from, sugar; as, glucic acid.
glisten: To sparkle or shine; especially, to shine with a mild, subdued, and fitful luster; to emit a soft, scintillating light; to gleam; as, the glistening stars. Syn. -- See Flash.
glottidean: Of or pertaining to the glottis; glottal.
glomerulus: The bunch of looped capillary blood vessels in a Malpighian capsule of the kidney.
glidingmachine: A construction consisting essentially of one or more aëroplanes for gliding in an inclined path from a height to the ground.
glioma: A tumor springing from the neuroglia or connective tissue of the brain, spinal cord, or other portions of the nervous system.
glutaeus: The great muscle of the buttock in man and most mammals, and the corresponding muscle in many lower animals. Note: In man, the glutæus is composed of three distinct parts, which extend and abduct the thigh, and help support the body in standing.
glede: The common European kite (Milvus ictinus). This name is also sometimes applied to the buzzard. [Written also glead, gled, gleed, glade, and glide.] | A live coal. (old) The cruel ire, red as any glede. Chaucer.
glycidic: Pertaining to, or derived from, glycide; as, glycidic acid.
gluey: Viscous; glutinous; of the nature of, or like, glue.
glyconic: Consisting of a spondee, a choriamb, and a pyrrhic; -- applied to a kind of verse in Greek and Latin poetry. -- n. (Pros.) A glyconic verse.
glycol: (a) A thick, colorless liquid, C2H4(OH)2, of a sweetish taste, produced artificially from certain ethylene compounds. It is a diacid alcohol, intermediate between ordinary ethyl alcohol and glycerin. (b) Any one of the large class of diacid alcohols, of which glycol proper is the type.
glossologist: One who defines and explains terms; one who is versed in glossology.
glaucous: 1. Of a sea-green color; of a dull green passing into grayish blue. Lindley. 2. (Bot.) Covered with a fine bloom or fine white powder easily rubbed off, as that on a blue plum, or on a cabbage leaf. Gray.
glaucus: A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks, found in the warmer latitudes, swimming in the open sea. These mollusks are beautifully colored with blue and silvery white.
glutination: The act of uniting with glue; sticking together.
glassful: The contents of a glass; as much of anything as a glass will hold. | Glassy; shining like glass. (old) "Minerva's glassful shield." Marston.
glossarist: A writer of glosses or of a glossary; a commentator; a scholiast. Tyrwhitt.
glutinate: To unite with glue; to cement; to stick together. Bailey.
glassrope: A remarkable vitreous sponge, of the genus Hyalonema, first brought from Japan. It has a long stem, consisting of a bundle of long and large, glassy, siliceous fibers, twisted together.
gladen: Sword grass; any plant with sword-shaped leaves, esp. the European Iris foetidissima. [Written also gladwyn, gladdon, and glader.]
gleaner: 1. One who gathers after reapers. 2. One who gathers slowly with labor. Locke.
glottology: The science of tongues or languages; comparative philology; glossology.
glonoin: 1. Same as Nitroglycerin; -- called also oil of glonoin. (old) 2. (Med.) A dilute solution of nitroglycerin used as a neurotic.
gladiatorial: Of or pertaining to gladiators, or to contests or combatants in general.
glutton: 1. One who eats voraciously, or to excess; a gormandizer. 2. Fig.: One who gluts himself. Gluttons in murder, wanton to destroy. Granville. 3. (Zoöl.) A carnivorous mammal (Gulo luscus), of the… | Gluttonous; greedy; gormandizing. "Glutton souls." Dryden. A glutton monastery in former ages makes a hungry ministry in our days. Fuller.
gley: To squint; to look obliquely; to overlook things. [Scot.] Jamieson.
gloom: 1. Partial or total darkness; thick shade; obscurity; as, the gloom of a forest, or of midnight. 2. A shady, gloomy, or dark place or grove. Before a gloom of stubborn-shafted oaks. Tennyson . 3. | 1. To shine or appear obscurely or imperfectly; to glimmer. 2. To become dark or dim; to be or appear dismal, gloomy, or sad; to come to the evening twilight. The black gibbet glooms beside the way.
glossic: A system of phonetic spelling based upon the present values of English letters, but invariably using one symbol to represent one sound only. Ingglish Glosik konvaiA. J. Ellis.
gluten: The viscid, tenacious substance which gives adhesiveness to dough. Note: Gluten is a complex and variable mixture of glutin or gliadin, vegetable fibrin, vegetable casein, oily material, etc., and ia a very nutritious element of food.
gloxinia: American genus of herbaceous plants with very handsome bell- shaped blossoms; -- named after B. P. Gloxin, a German botanist.
glimpse: 1. A sudden flash; transient luster. LIght as the lightning glimpse they ran. Milton. 2. A short, hurried view; a transitory or fragmentary perception; a quick sight. | to appear by glimpses; to catch glimpses. Drayton.
globe: 1. A round or spherical body, solid or hollow; a body whose surface is in every part equidistant from the center; a ball; a sphere. 2. Anything which is nearly spherical or globular in shape; | To gather or form into a globe.
glutazine: A nitrogenous substance, forming a heavy, sandy powder, white or nearly so. It is a derivative of pyridine.
glabellum: The median, convex lobe of the head of a trilobite. See Trilobite.
glossography: The writing of glossaries, glosses, or comments for illustrating an author.
glycerite: A medicinal preparation made by mixing or dissolving a substance in glycerin.
glycyrrhiza: 1. (Bot.) A genus of papilionaceous herbaceous plants, one species of which (G. glabra), is the licorice plant, the roots of which have a bittersweet mucilaginous taste. 2. (Med.) The root of Glycyrrhiza glabra (liquorice root), used as a demulcent, etc.
glazing: 1. The act or art of setting glass; the art of covering with a vitreous or glasslike substance, or of polishing or rendering glossy. 2. The glass set, or to be set, in a sash, frame. etc. 3. The glass, glasslike, or glossy substance with which any surface is incrusted or overlaid; as, the glazing of pottery or porcelain, or of paper. 4.
glucosuria: A condition in which glucose is discharged in the urine; diabetes mellitus.
glossiness: The condition or quality of being glossy; the luster or brightness of a smooth surface. Boyle.
glib: 1. Smooth; slippery; as, ice is glib. (old) 2. Speaking or spoken smoothly and with flippant rapidity; fluent; voluble; as, a glib tongue; a glib speech. I want that glib and oily art, To speak and… | A thick lock of hair, hanging over the eyes. (old) The Irish have, from the Scythians, mantles and long glibs, which is a thick curied bush of hair hanging down over their eyes, and monstrously…
glossoepiglottic: Pertaining to both tongue and epiglottis; as, glossoepiglottic folds.
glacier: An immense field or stream of ice, formed in the region of perpetual snow, and moving slowly down a mountain slope or valley, as in the Alps, or over an extended area, as in Greenland. Note: The mass of compacted snow forming the upper part of a glacier is called the firn, or névé;
glacis: A gentle slope, or a smooth, gently sloping bank; especially (Fort.), that slope of earth which inclines from the covered way toward the exterior ground or country (see Illust. of Ravelin).
glanderous: Of or pertaining to glanders; of the nature of glanders. Youatt.
glycoluril: A white, crystalline, nitrogenous substance, obtained by the reduction of allantoïn.
glynne: A glen. See Glen. Note: [Obs. singly, but occurring often in locative names in Ireland, as Glen does in Scotland.] He could not beat out the Irish, yet he did shut them up within those narrow corners and glyns under the mountain's foot. Spenser.
glissade: A sliding, as down a snow slope in the Alps. Tyndall.
glycyrrhizimic: From, or pertaining to, glycyrrhizin; as, glycyrrhizimic acid.
glassen: Glassy; glazed. (old) And pursues the dice with glassen eyes. B. Jonson.
glyph: A sunken channel or groove, usually vertical. See Triglyph.
glottis: The opening from the pharynx into the larynx or into the trachea. See Larynx.
gluteal: Pertaining to, or in the region of, the glutæus.
gluepot: A utensil for melting glue, consisting of an inner pot holding the glue, immersed in an outer one containing water which is heated to soften the glue.
glabreate: To make smooth, plain, or bare. (old)
globulite: A rudimentary form of crystallite, spherical in shape.
glutin: 1. Same as Gliadin. 2. Sometimes synonymous with Gelatin.
glout: To pout; to look sullen. (old) Garth. | To view attentively; to gloat on; to stare at. (old) Wright.
gladness: State or quality of being glad; pleasure; joyful satisfaction; cheerfulness. They . . . did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart. Acts ii. 46. Note: Gladness is rarely or never equivalent to mirth, merriment, gayety, and triumph, and it usually expresses less than delight. It sometimes expresses great joy. The Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day.
glower: to look intently; to stare angrily or with a scowl. Thackeray.
glooming: Twilight (of morning or evening); the gloaming. When the faint glooming in the sky First lightened into day. Trench. The balmy glooming, crescent-lit. Tennyson.
gloppen: To surprise or astonish; to be startled or astonished. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
glairin: A glairy viscous substance, which forms on the surface of certain mineral waters, or covers the sides of their inclosures; -- called also baregin.
glazer: 1. One who applies glazing, as in pottery manufacture, etc.; one who gives a glasslike or glossy surface to anything; a calenderer or smoother of cloth, paper, and the like. 2. A tool or machine used in glazing, polishing, smoothing, etc.; amoung cutlers and lapidaries, a wooden wheel covered with emery, or having a band of lead and tin alloy, for polishing cutlery, etc.
glacial: 1. Pertaining to ice or to its action; consisting of ice; frozen; icy; esp., pertaining to glaciers; as, glacial phenomena. Lyell. 2. (Chem.) Resembling ice; having the appearance and consistency of ice; - - said of certain solid compounds; as, glacial phosphoric or acetic acids.
glycerine: An oily, viscous liquid, C3H5(OH)3, colorless and odorless, and with a hot, sweetish taste, existing in the natural fats and oils as the base, combined with various acids, as oleic, margaric, stearic, and palmitic. It is a triatomic alcohol, and hence is also called glycerol. See Note under Gelatin.
glyceryl: A compound radical, C3H5, regarded as the essential radical of glycerin. It is metameric with allyl. Called also propenyl.
glandered: Affected with glanders; as, a glandered horse. Yu
gleed: A live or glowing coal; a glede. (old) Chaucer. Longfellow.
glauconite: The green mineral characteristic of the greensand of the chalk and other formations. It is a hydrous silicate of iron and potash. See Greensand.
glaze: 1. To furnish (a window, a house, a sash, a ease, etc.) with glass. Two cabinets daintily paved, richly handed, and glazed with crystalline glass. Bacon. 2. To incrust, cover, or overlay with a thin… | 1. The vitreous coating of pottery or porcelain; anything used as a coating or color in glazing. See Glaze, v. t., 3. Ure. 2. (Cookery) Broth reduced by boiling to a gelatinous paste, and spread…
glance: 1. A sudden flash of light or splendor. Swift as the lightning glance. Milton. 2. A quick cast of the eyes; a quick or a casual look; a swift survey; a glimpse. Dart not scornful glances from those… | 1. To shoot or emit a flash of light; to shine; to flash. From art, from nature, from the schools, Let random influences glance, Like light in many a shivered lance, That breaks about the dappled…
glandulosity: Quality of being glandulous; a collection of glands. Sir T. Browne.
gliadin: Vegetable glue or gelatin; glutin. It is one of the constituents of wheat gluten, and is a tough, amorphous substance, which resembles animal glue or gelatin.
glissette: The locus described by any point attached to a curve that slips continuously on another fixed curve, the movable curve having no rotation at any instant.
glossy: 1. Smooth and shining; reflecting luster from a smooth surface; highly polished; lustrous; as, glossy silk; a glossy surface. 2. Smooth; specious; plausible; as, glossy deceit.
glasseye: 1. (Zoöl.) A fish of the great lakes; the wall-eyed pike. 2. (Far.) A species of blindness in horses in which the eye is bright and the pupil dilated; a sort of amaurosis. Youatt.
glycide: A colorless liquid, obtained from certain derivatives of glycerin, and regarded as a partially dehydrated glycerin; -- called also glycidic alcohol.
glosser: A polisher; one who gives a luster. | A writer of glosses; a scholiast; a commentator. L. Addison.
glassy: 1. Made of glass; vitreous; as, a glassy substance. Bacon. 2. Resembling glass in its properties, as in smoothness, brittleness, or transparency; as, a glassy stream; a glassy surface; the glassy deep. 3. Dull; wanting life or fire; lackluster; -- said of the eyes. "In his glassy eye." Byron. Glassy feldspar (Min.), a variety of orthoclase; sanidine.
glasswort: A seashore plant of the Spinach family (Salicornia herbacea), with succulent jointed stems; also, a prickly plant of the same family (Salsola Kali), both formerly burned for the sake of the ashes, which yield soda for making glass and soap.
